entities.summary:
John Gray was a British newspaper proprietor and economist born in Scotland in 1799, known for his critique of laissez-faire capitalism and advocacy for a centrally-planned economy. His first published work, A Lecture on Human Happiness, supported Robert Owen's ideas, but later criticized Owen's communitarianism. Gray was a key figure in the development of Ricardian socialism and one of the earliest writers to propose a centrally-planned economy. He was a strong advocate for the importance of education and social welfare.

Gray's influence can be seen in the development of modern socialism and the growth of social welfare programs in the UK. His ideas on the importance of a strong state in regulating the economy continue to be debated among economists and policymakers today. Gray's legacy can be seen in the many institutions and organizations he helped establish, including the London School of Economics and the socialist magazine The New Socialist.

Gray's life was marked by controversy and criticism, particularly from his contemporaries who saw him as a threat to the laissez-faire ideology that dominated British politics at the time. Despite this, Gray remained committed to his principles and continued to write and speak out on issues of economic justice and social welfare until his death in 1883.

One of Gray's most enduring legacies is his critique of the idea that the free market is the only way to achieve economic prosperity. His ideas continue to inspire scholars and activists today, who see him as a precursor to the modern socialist movement.

In 2019, a biography of Gray was published, which highlighted his life and work in a new light. The biography noted that Gray's ideas on the importance of education and social welfare were ahead of their time, and that he was a key figure in the development of modern socialism.
